text: Presidential elections were held in France on 5 December 1965, with a second round on 19 December. They were the first direct presidential elections in the Fifth Republic and the first since the Second Republic in 1848. This was the second presidential election since the beginning of the Fifth Republic. Under the first draft of the 1958 constitution, the president was to be elected by an electoral college to appease concerns about de Gaulle's allegedly authoritarian or Bonapartist tendencies, as there had been a historical reluctance in France to have a directly elected president due to Louis-Napoléon Bonaparte's 1851 coup d'état before the end of his term. However, a direct presidential election had always been essential to de Gaulle's political vision, and he had it adopted by the 1962 referendum. When the electoral campaign started, most political commentators believed de Gaulle would win re-election in a single round, leading opposition leaders to be reluctant to challenge him. Some potential candidates, such as former Prime Minister Pierre Mendès-France, declined to run due to their opposition to direct presidential elections. De Gaulle did not expect a significant challenger, announced his candidacy only one month before the first round, and did not lead an active campaign. The centre-left paper L'Express campaigned for a non-Communist opposition candidate; one potential challenger was Gaston Defferre, Mayor of Marseille and an internal opponent of SFIO leader Guy Mollet, who led a coalition of the SFIO, the Radical Party, and the centre-right MRP. Nevertheless, the leaders of these parties refused to support his candidacy. Defferre's failed candidacy led to other politicians entering the race. MRP leader Jean Lecanuet was nominated by his party and the CNIP to represent the centre, running a liberal and pro-European campaign influenced by John F. Kennedy, criticizing de Gaulle's "archaism" and "nationalism" to appeal to younger and more moderate conservatives. François Mitterrand, a former Fourth Republic minister not belonging to any party, offered to run as the sole candidate of the left. Mitterrand had been an opponent of de Gaulle since 1958, like the Communists but contrary to the SFIO leadership, and had written the book The Permanent Coup d'État, strongly criticizing de Gaulle's policies. He obtained support from several left-wing parties, including the French Communist Party (PCF), which wished to end its isolation. Despite a lacklustre campaign, de Gaulle won the first round by over three million votes but fell short of a majority, forcing a runoff two weeks later against Mitterrand. Tixier-Vignancour supported Mitterrand in the second round, and Lecanuet urged his voters not to vote for de Gaulle. De Gaulle defeated Mitterrand by a decisive margin in the runoff, though Mitterrand performed better than expected, signaling one of the first warnings that de Gaulle's popularity was waning. De Gaulle retained his Prime Minister Georges Pompidou but decided to carry out a cabinet reshuffle, dismissing his Economy Minister Valéry Giscard d'Estaing, which damaged relations within the majority coalition with Giscard's party, the Independent Republicans, the last allies of the Gaullists.
